writableLeaves.currentText: Strongest feature: Evans presents a concrete worked example encompassing oldest-manuscript absence, Gospel comparison, critical bracketing, acceptance of interpolation, proposed omission, and a proportionate question about substantive consequence. Principal limitation: One detectable gloss cannot establish whole-text accuracy, and teaching-level resilience does not answer Ehrman’s decisive concern that no surviving witnesses reveal the earliest copying period. Live burden: Evans must justify extrapolation from identifiable later interpolations to preservation across undocumented generations and address whether non-original sayings matter independently of doctrinal redundancy. Locked score: The 83 combines outstanding 89-point evidence, 91-point clarity, and 91-point calibration with good coherence, but the adjudicated 69 responsiveness and 80 relevance scores record incomplete contact with the missing-earliest-copies argument and only partial support for broader preservation.

sourceEvidence.speaker: Craig Evans
sourceEvidence.excerpt: here is what I have written I believe the gospels have been accurately preserved down through the centuries though I suppose some Skeptics could say something to this effect we don't have the originals of Matthew or of Paul's letters or of any book of the New Testament what we have are copies of these books most copies are hundreds of years after the originals and all of them have differences in them scribes would change the gospels to reflect their own View and so on and so forth examples of this could include I suppose Luke 22:43 to 44 which tells us an angel ministered to Jesus while he was in prayer in Gethsemane and that sweat like drops of blood fell from his brow our oldest manuscripts do not have these verses moreover nothing like these verses occurs in the other gospels textual critics and commentators suspect these verses represent a later scribal gloss a dramatic embellishment of the scene as it were perhaps even an upgrade of Jesus's Divine status in their addition of the Greek New Testament Bruce Meer and his colleagues rightly plac these verses in square brackets indicating that they doubt very much they were in the original I agree with their decision if we all agree and so omit these verses from Luke's gospel have we lost a significant element of the passion story or of the Divine status of Jesus so clearly taught elsewhere no the ending of Mark's gospel
sourceEvidence.proposition: Known interpolations such as Luke's bloody-sweat passage can be identified and omitted without losing a significant teaching about Jesus.

responseComponents.text: Concedes late glosses but argues that identifying and removing a disputed passage does not eliminate a significant teaching or passion element.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Removing a detectable gloss can preserve broader teaching, though not prove whole-text accuracy.
logicalCoherence.adjudicationRationale: The reasoning coherently limits the consequence of a detectable gloss, but it does not establish accurate preservation of the text as a whole.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Luke's disputed verses, oldest-manuscript absence, and critical bracketing provide a concrete worked example.
evidenceWarrant.adjudicationRationale: The move supplies a concrete passage, its absence from the oldest manuscripts, comparison with other Gospels, and explicit critical bracketing.

responsiveness.rationale: It addresses the consequence of one gloss but not Ehrman's missing-earliest-copies argument.
responsiveness.adjudicationRationale: It answers the significance of one identifiable gloss but does not resolve the target argument about unavailable originals and earliest copies.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move supports teaching-level resilience while only partly supporting accurate preservation.
relevanceBurden.adjudicationRationale: The example strongly supports resilience of a significant teaching, while only partially supporting Evans's broader accurate-preservation burden.

precisionClarity.rationale: The passage, manuscript fact, critical judgment, and proposed consequence are all distinctly stated.
precisionClarity.adjudicationRationale: The passage, manuscript evidence, textual-critical conclusion, proposed omission, and claimed consequence are each distinctly stated.

calibrationCharity.rationale: Evans presents the skeptical case accurately, accepts the interpolation, and asks a proportionate significance question.
calibrationCharity.adjudicationRationale: Evans fairly presents the skeptical textual case, accepts the interpolation, and confines his conclusion to its limited substantive significance.

writableLeaves.currentText: Strongest feature: Ehrman precisely redirects the significance inquiry from whether doctrine survives to whether words placed in Jesus’s mouth were originally present, using two famous sayings from a conceded interpolation. Principal limitation: The large raw number of textual differences may exaggerate substantive uncertainty, and one prominent passage cannot independently establish the prevalence of saying-level misattribution. Live burden: Evans must explain why recoverable identification and removal answer the historical misquotation itself, while Ehrman must establish how representative such cases are of the New Testament’s portrayal. Locked score: The 92 reflects extraordinary coherence, warrant, 95-point responsiveness, 94-point relevance, 92-point precision, and strong calibration, making this the clearest motion-specific reply because it accepts shared textual premises and exposes doctrinal survival as an incomplete metric.

sourceEvidence.proposition: Textual variants materially affect which familiar sayings can truthfully be attributed to Jesus, even when they do not create a doctrine.

responseComponents.text: Uses the admitted non-original adultery passage to argue that variants remove familiar sayings attributed to Jesus and therefore matter to the motion.
